(the sound /ʔa/) ;The “Olive Branch” dictionary gives an interesting explanation of this, focusing on its phonetic quality asaprefix in the following three situations (as applies to the Palestinian dialect):1. Prefix indicating the past tense of the form أفعل (a pattern that largely has disappeared from the Levantine colloquials). Ex: أَهْمَل (he neglected).2. Prefix indicating the comparative / superlative; (such as أَكْبَر and أَحْلَى).3. Prefix indicating the first person singular (I) of the verb in the imperfect tense. Note that if preceded byaconsonant, the full hamza is preserved, whereas if preceded byavowel, the hamza is swallowed and only the fatha remains. Also, when preceded by ب of the imperfect tense (habitual mood), the hamza is again swallowed by the fatha retained. As in:biddy afuut (بدي اْفُوت) = I want to come in3a∫aan 2afuut (عشان أَفُوت ) = so that I can go inlaazem 2afuut (لازِم أَفُوت) = I must go inbakteb (بَكْتِب) = I writebat3allam (بَتْعَلَّم) = I learn[pronunciation: ʔa]

In general, Brustad states that the more “hypothetical” the situation, the more likely the speaker is to use the perfective tense, in order to put “distance” between himself/herself and the expectation that the statement is true or could be realized. Hence, Brustad provides the following scale as a guideline.إذا + كان + الماضي counterfactual ;إذا + الماضي punctual hypothetical;إذا + المضارع / جملة بدون فعل : stative hypothetical;These are guidlines only.note it is common to use ب in the then-clause, even if the first clause is in the past tense. This is because ب is used as a future tense marker in the Levantine dialects (and this stands in marked contrast to the Egyptian dialect);[pronunciation: ʔi∂a]
  2. إذا + كان + الماضي : irrealis / connterfactual conditional: if (like if I were fish, or if I had gone to the store yesterday, when if fact one did not go to the store yesterday) ;using لو as an irrealis conditional is not necessarily a fixed rule, the way it is in CA.note that the كان here is usually used, and it’s role is more to put distance between the speaker’s “expectation” of the statement being realized or true.[pronunciation: ʔi∂a]
  3. إذَا + الماض : if (punctual hypothetical) [pronunciation: ʔi∂a][keyword]
  4. إذَا + المضارع : stative hypothetical: if ;these verbs are usually marked either with عم or ب .sometimes this is called a “non-hypothetical conditional mood”, because it is a sentence in which the if statement (the protasis) is assumed true or to have a high degree of expectation that it is true.[pronunciation: ʔi∂a][keyword]
  5. إذَا + جملة بدون فعل : stative hypothetical: ifsometimes this is called a “non-hypothetical conditional mood”, because it is a sentence in which the if statement (the protasis) is assumed true or to have a high degree of expectation that it is true.   6. إذَا كان : frozen structure used in conditionals. in other words, the كان does not conjugate, but simply stays as كان. Rather, the past tense of كان is sometimes used to put distance between the speaker and the event. [pronunciation: ʔi∂a]

1. nouns in the Levantine dialect often take he plural form ـات . Although in some cases it is a counting plural (see شعرات), this can even be used with words where the plural would be unexpected. Kristen Brustad calls the latter حَليبات plurals, from the phrase شْراب حَلِيباتَك (drink your milk! See her article of the same title).In the حليبات plural cases, the ـات ending gives a degree of individuation, and is often accompanied by suffix pronouns or in an إضافة , or marked with the demonstrative ها. Objects are often sometimes with a لَ to emphasize their individuation. These plurals often refer to something in the immediate vicinity of having immediate relevance to the speech act. They are often treated as plurals (even in the case of something like حليبات), further showing their individuation and contextual relevance. Lastly, given the specificity of thet noun, it usually only refers to one "batch" of something. "Batch" does not refer to amount, but rather some sense it all belongs together (i.e. a specific person's money, even if it is a lot of money). Brustad also argues that there is a diminuitive quality to حليبات plurals (depending on context), emphasizing the smallness of the amount in question, and hence also expressing things like cuteness or disdain (depending on context). 1. relative pronoun: who, which, that ;This replaces all the different relative pronouns from CA. in other words, there is masculine/feminine specific or singular/dual/plural specific relative pronoun in CA, they are have all been replaced by this. In CA see الذي، التي and so forth.Note that, just like in CA, the clause after the relative pronoun should have a resumptive pronoun (i.e. one that refers back to the original noun that اللي is referring two). However, there are two exceptions. The first is if the relative clause contains a participle that is acting as a verb, and if the subject of the participle is the same as what اللي refers to, then a resumptive pronoun is often “understood” to be a part of the participle. As in: السِتّ اللي ساكْنة عَ الناصْيَة the woman who lives on the corner. This is the same as in CA when a verb is used in the relative clause. The second is if the relative clause is just a prepositional phrase, like الكتاب اللي عَ الكُرْسي (the book that is on the chair), there is no need for a relative pronoun.note that يللي is typically listed in Syrian and some Lebanese sources, and اللي or للي listed in Palestinian sources. At the end of the day, since the initial vowel is often dropped, they sound very similar.[pronunciation: illy / 'il-ly][keyword]
  2. relative pronoun: who, which, that ; (more examples)[keyword]

Brustad points out that the following example is considered incorrect: نِمْتِ كْوَيِّسِ اْللي اْتْحَسَّنِ الجَوّ (I slept well since that weather has improved). She suggests that the reason for this is that اِللي must act as a conjunction in cases of emotional reaction, such as happiness, anger, relief, or resentment. “The relativized /illi/ clause is linked to that emotional state in that it contains the reason or cause of that state. The /illi/ clause thus becomes a relative clause modifying an underlying or understood reason or cause for the emotional state.” She suggests that it could be used in cases of highly individuated nouns (i.e. people, god, etc.), rather than un-individuated nouns (e.g. the weather). J. Elihay says it is used in expressions of satisfaction, pleasure, sorry, etc.[pronunciation: illy / 'il-ly]

  2. Indicative mood marker with durative, habitual, gnomic, and performative verbs: ب is used to mark present tense verbs (فعل مضارع ) to show actuality or duration. The correct usage of this does depend on the nature of the verb and what you are trying to say. When studying this, one should always consider the tense and aspect one wants to use. For instance, بِيْشُوف would be habitual in meaning, whereas if one wants to to say “seeing”, شايِف is the correct form.A much simpler explanation:ب is a prefix attached to verbs to show present tense (or future tense, see below). In the present tense, in tends to show habitual action, whereas عم shows an ongoing or continuous action (the “-ing” ending in English is usually used to translate عم).Present tense verbs will not take ب if there is another word modifying them or “controlling” the tense or linguistic mood of a sentence. Hence, when preceded by a word like لازم (must), the following verb will not have ب . Compare:بِدُّو يْفُوت : he wants to come in ;لازِم يْفُوت : he must come in;بيفُوت : he comes in (or he will come in);
  3. Indicative mood marker showing a change in state. This form is specifically used after a temporal verb (Such as صار), in which case the temporal verb emphasizes that a (new) state is being entered ;compare these two sentences:اِبْنِي صار بْيِسْبَح لَحالُه [L] my son has started to swim by himself;نِزِل عَ البِرْكِة وْصار يِسْبَح [L] he went into the pool and started swimming;the first sentence shows that now, the son is able to swim by himself, i.e. صار shows that one is entering into that general reality. In contrast, the second sentence puts the emphasis on the start of a single action;
  4. عم + ب + فعل مضارع : Indicative mood marker to show progressive tense: used to mark present tense verbs (فعل مضارع ) to show the the progressive tense (translated as -ing in English). Note that at times the form is just عم + فعل مضارع ( i.e. the ب is left out). Brustad implies that there is no differences (p.247), and perhaps the usage is simply one of dialect or phonetic preference.
  5. فعل مضارع بدون علامة + عم + ب + فعل مضارع : embedding عم ب inside of an unmarked present tense verb can imply a past habitual reading. This is specifically used with non-punctual verbs (i.e. stative or habitual verbs). Brustad gives an example (p.240), but does not dwell on this much. I'm calling it an implied past habitual, though, because the use of a verb without ب (such as يكونوا ) can be read as “they would be”, and then the specificity of عم ب pulls out a specific instance. So essentially the speaker is giving a “possible example” of what was a regular event. (compare how one would translate كانوا بيعملوا (they used to do...) and يكونوا عم بيعملوا (they would be doing...) ;
  6. intentive future marker: willBrustad argues this is a future tense used to show intent, used with non-factual information. (compare with رَح). However, since the usage seems to vary across dialects, making generalizations seems hard. According to Brustad, some notes about using it:1. used with questions that show intention, hence it is often on the first or second person verb, e.g. in questions, to show intention ;2. cannot be used to ask about factual information unless it focuses on addresses intentions. it would be incorrect to say:شُوْ بِتْجِيب مَعَك [L] what will you bring with you;but you are allowed to say:اِمْتَى بِتْزِيد لْنا المَعَاش [L] when do you plan to raise our salary;3. There is clearly some overlap between رح and ب, and it also varies some between regions in the Levant.4. note also that some sentences have similar meanings with and without ب :وَعَدْني إِنُّه بْيِرْجَع [S] He promised me he would come back;وَعَدْني إِنُّه يِرْجَع [S] He promised me to come back;
  7. deonitic mood marker: ب is used in polite questions, to show possibility, and is often translated as might, could, would.
  8. with رَح : At times, verbs will take two markers, رَح + ب ;This does not seem to change the meaning at all.
  9. commitive mood: used in negation to mean “this will not happen”, i.e. it is committing to the intention that this will not happen ;
  10. intentive future used in conditionals ;
  11. ب + فعل مضارع : used with verbs of knowing (like “to know”, “to remember”, etc.). In this case the verb is durative (stative). This is in marked contrast to the Egyptian dialect, which uses participles. Levantine arabic seems to use both participles and verbs with ب, depending on context.compare use of عارف and بعرف. Brustad suggests that the used of ب with عرف suggests that there is a process of learning, and hence in the examples with ب, there is often a “body of knowledge” that needs to be learned. In contrast, the participle is used to indicate a resultant state that has special relevance to the speech act. Compare these examples:
  12. Subjunctive mood: DOES NOT TaKE ب . The subjunctive mood shows possibility or desirability (often translated as would or could). The subjunctive indicates “unrealized verbal action” or a “potential event without reference – or speaker commitment – to actualization.”
  13. polite questions in Syrian do not always take ب . (this needs to be further explored. see the one example and conflicting information).
  14. definiteness or individuation of a subject can affect the use of ب or not. Essentially, indefinite, less individuated nouns are less likely to take ب . This makes sense if one recalls that ب is used to refer to actual events, and that when speaking indefinite nouns are often used in theoretical statements (like “what if someone ate a whole cake”).

1. Barjees, Barsees(a kind of board game. It is played on a cloth board and six cowrie shells, called وَدَع, are thrown as dice. There are two players, each having four pieces. One player's pieces have the head of a horse or rooster and thus are called حْصُون or دْيُوك , and the second player's pieces have a dome like head like a soldier's helmet and so are sometimes called جْنُود , but alternatively are also called أَرْگِيلة , i.e. a hookah. There are also other names for the pieces depending on area.Players alternate turns. On each turn, the player throws the six ودع , and depending on how they land moves one of his pieces accordingly. There are six possible ways the shells can fall:شَكِّة : all six shells face up. Player can move six squares and gets to roll againدَسْت، ج دْسُوْت : one shell face down. Player can move 10 + 1. The 1 is called a خال can be used to bring a piece into play. Player gets to roll again.اتنين أو دواق : two shells face down. Player can move two.ثلاثة : three shells face down. Player can move three.أربعة : four shells face down. Player can move four.بَنْج، ج بْنُوْج : five shells face down. Player can move 25 + 1. The 1 is called a خال can be used to bring a piece into play. Player gets to roll again.بَاْرَة، ج بَاْرَاْت : all six shells are face down. Player can move 12 squares and gets to roll again.The goal of the game is to move one's pieces around the board and back to the starting point, and then into the large central square, sometimes called المَطْبَخ / the kitchen. The first player to get all his pieces around wins. Players can also eliminate the other player's pieces by landing on them, in which the eliminated piece and goes back to the beginning and needs to be brought back into play with a خال. Certain squares, marked by an X, are deemed safe and are called قَلْعَة / castle ; a player sitting on a castle cannot be eliminated.Barjees is derived from the game Pachisi that originated in India. The name Pachisi comes from Hindu word paccīs, meaning twenty-five, and the game is played with cowrie shells just like Barjees. It is also worth nothing that the numbers for the rolls, like دست and بارة, are from Hindi. There are many Westernized versions of the game Pachisi, such as Sorry! and Parcheesi.) Arabic texts trace the name of the game in Arabic, Barjees, to name of the planet Jupiter in Farsi, that being بَرْجِيس, which is supposed to represent luck. Alternatively, Yassine Abdelrahim traces it to the word بَرجستن, which means to jump.Given the similarity to the name of the US-made game Parcheesi, there may be another origin to the word, but when searching I couldn't find a clear explanation of where the name Parcheesi comes from besides Pachisi. John Hamilton, who is credited with bringing the game to the US in 1867, registered it as Patcheesi, and the name was changed to Parcheesi a year or so later, according to online sources. The "r" could have been added just to sound more foreign, or perhaps was meant to represent a retroflex r. Hamilton sold the rights to the game to a company that would later be known as Selchow & Righter. A court case about the name states: "The Hindoostanee name for it might be pronounced 'Parchise,' 'Pucheese,' or 'Putcheesx,' but not 'Parcheesi'" and that "their predecessors made up this particular name merely as a changed form of the sound or pronunciation of the Hindoostanee name of the game" even though it is "similar to the old name." Although it sounds a bit like a legal workaround for the game makers, as far as the Arabic name is concerned, Parcheesi may be derived directly from an Indian pronunciation of the name Pachisi, in which case Barjees could be related to that rather than to Farsi.)

  3. Aleppo, the city in northwestern Syria. It was known in antiquity as Khalpe, Khalibon, and to the Greeks and Romans as Beroea (Βέροια). During the Crusades, and again during the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon, the name alep was used. "aleppo" is the Italianised version of this.In arabic the ancient name Halab has been preserved. It is of obscure origin. Some have proposed that Halab means 'iron' or 'copper' in amorite languages, since it was a major source of these metals in antiquity. However, according to the 20th-century historian sheikh Kamel al-Ghazzi and contemporary linguist priest Barsoum ayyoub, the name Halab (and consequently aleppo) is derived from the aramaic word Halaba which means white, referring to the colour of soil and marble abundant in the area. The modern-day arabic nickname of the city, ash-Shahbaa (arabic: الشهباء), which means "the white-coloured", is also derived from the famous white marble of aleppo.There is a legend / myth that the name Halab means "gave out milk", coming from the ancient tradition that abraham gave milk to travelers as they passed through the region. The colour of his cows was white (arabic: شهباء shahbaa), therefore the city was also called Halab ash-Shahbaa ("he milked the white-coloured"). [pronunciation: ḥalab]

Six main types of Dabka in Palestine include:al-Shamaliyya (الشمالية): is probably the most famous type of dabke. It consists of a lawweeh (لويح) at the head of a group of men holding hands and formed in a semicircle.al-Sha’rawiyya (الشعراوية): is limited to men and is characterized by strong steps or stomps. The lawweeh is the most important element in this type of dabke.al-Karaadiyya (الكرادية): is characterized by a lack of a lawweeh and slow movement with an azif (عازف) (flute player) in the middle of the circle.al-Farah (الفره): is one of the most active types of dabke and therefore requires a high degree of physical fitness.al-Ghazal (الغزل): is characterized by three strong stomps of the right foot, and is usually tiring for those dancing.al-Sahja (السحجة): is a popular Palestinian and Jordanian dance which became significantly more popular during the British Mandate for Palestine. al-Sahja belongs mostly to northern and central Palestine, and in the south has two kinds:as-Samir (السامر) and al-Dahiyya (الدحية). as-Samir's form involves 2 rows of men on opposite walls, competing with folk poetry, sometimes improvised and even exchanging insults, competing in cleverness of retorts. al-Dahiyya is a Bedouin version of the same kind in which there is a professional dancer that dances between the two opposing walls of men who are competing for her attention, and at times give her money. al-Sahja usually occurs the night before the wedding party of the groom (zafat al-'arees), with most of the men in the village participating, especially those who will be attending or are directly involved in the other wedding festivities.One of the famous songs, called على دلعونا, meaning “let's go help”, according to folk tradition comes from the time when house roofs were made of wood, straw, and dirt, which required stomping the dirt in a uniform way to compact it evenly. Hence the word for cooperation (تعاون) led to the phrase على دلعونا ;See also فوكلور العرس والغناء الشعبي: ليلة الحناء لهشام عارف الموعد ومأمون أحمد الموعد ;[pronunciation: dabke]

1. Fareekeh. Which is a cereal food made from green wheat that goes through a roasting process in its production. The wheat is harvested while the grains are yellow and the seeds are still soft ; it is then piled and sun-dried. The piles are then carefully set on fire so only the straw and chaff burn and not the seeds. It is the high moisture content of the seeds that prevents them from burning. The now roasted wheat undergoes further thrashing and sun-drying to make the flavor, texture, and color uniform. It is this thrashing or rubbing process of the grains that gives this food its name, farīk or “rubbed.” The seeds are now cracked into smaller pieces so they look like a green bulgur.(In Iraq it is called القرة خرمان and in Egypt فريك );
